title: Tanzania blast fishing getting out of control
article_text:
Tanzania blast fishing getting out of control
The East African
September 13, 2014 Saturday


Copyright 2014 The East African All Rights Reserved
Length: 424 words
Body


  Blast fishing  the practice by which fishermen use explosives to stun and catch fish  is rapidly getting out of control in Tanzania, endangering the remaining coastal coral reefs and putting the livelihood of thousands of artesanal fishermen at risk, a new report says.  "If this illegal practice is not stopped, gradually Tanzania could easily end up with a wasteland of ocean," said Michael Markovina an officer with SmartFish, an EU funded programme which produced the report.  Already fisherman who use ordinary ring nets say their catches have been affected and the number of fish has drastically reduced. 
  The explosives fishermen use are usually made from readily available cheap craft components such as fertilisers. They are dropped overboard off the coast of Tanzania and Zanzibar with the resulting bomb blast destroying corals, fish larvae and eggs.   Another horrific consequence is the frequent sight of fishermen in Tanzania walking around with missing limbs.  Accidents happen because explosives are usually lit with small fuses and tossed overboard. The underwater shock waves produced by the explosion stun the fish, rupturing their swim bladders  the organ which helps control their buoyancy. So they float to the surface and are then scooped up by waiting nets.   According to Smart Fish, a fisheries programme funded by the European Union, Tanzania is the only country in Africa where fishing using explosives still occurs on a large scale.    Although it is illegal, it occurs along the entire Tanzanian coastline, from Mtwara to Tanga, and off nearby islands. There have also been reports of blast fishing off north Zanzibar.  Dynamite fishing began in the 1960s but by the 1990s it had been brought under control. Over the past five years, however, it has been increasing.   All blast fishing was banned in 2003 with a minimum sentence of five years for dynamite fishing and 12 months for possession of explosives, but it has boomed in recent years.  The report says that it is very difficult to track down the illegal fishermen as they are very secretive about their operations.   Local fishermen have informed the police about those who use the crude fishing method, but it has not stemmed the practice. They say that those arrested pay a bribe and come back, and if they find out who reported them they threaten retribution.  Besides, the perpetrators are not afraid of being sentenced because  blast fishing is such a lucrative business as only one blast can lead to a catch of up to 400kg and a profit of $1,800.
